title: EvoRouter: Cost-Efficient Multi-Agent Routing via Insight-Guided On-Policy Distillation
summary: Serving web queries at scale with multi-agent systems requires jointly configuring large language models, collaboration modes, agent counts, interaction rounds, and skills. However, the resulting configuration space grows combinatorially, while sparse execution rewards provide limited fine-grained supervision for interdependent planning decisions. We propose EvoRouter, a self-evolving multi-agent routing framework driven by insight-guided on-policy distillation. A dedicated expert periodically synthesizes performance-cost feedback from configuration trajectories across tasks into reusable conditional routing insights about capability requirements, returns from resource scaling, and interactions among configuration choices. A privileged teacher combines these evolving insights with current execution feedback to provide dense token-level supervision for the router's own planning trajectories through on-policy distillation. Cost-aware reinforcement learning jointly optimizes task performance and computational cost. Together, these training signals internalize execution insights into the routing policy. The updated policy generates new trajectories that support subsequent insight extraction, forming an execution-driven self-improvement loop. We evaluate EvoRouter on 19 in-domain datasets spanning five domains and two out-of-domain benchmarks. EvoRouter achieves an average in-domain accuracy of 68.69%, outperforming the strongest routing baseline by 7.23 percentage points while reducing inference compute cost by 50.95%. Our code is open-sourced at https://github.com/CenYangtze/EvoRouter.

title: Metacognitive Decoding: Efficient Inference for Diffusion Language Agents
summary: Diffusion language models offer a promising path to efficient agents through parallel token generation. However, efficient interaction requires adapting both where computation is spent and how much text is generated. We introduce a metacognitive controller that guides diffusion generation according to the needs of the current response and the agent's interaction with the environment. It learns when to finalize tokens and how far generation should extend, reducing overall computation within responses. Our controller, a lightweight plug-in for the diffusion backbone, is trained on agent trajectories to balance correctness and generation cost. This approach connects the agent's generation process to the interaction the agent serves. Experiments across five benchmarks demonstrate that our approach reduces inference FLOPs by 20.6% on average compared with the most efficient baseline, while maintaining competitive task accuracy. Ablation studies further validate the effectiveness of our approach.

title: Remembering Is Not Enough: Refining Memories and Learning When to Use Them in Multi-Agent Systems
summary: Memory helps LLM-based multi-agent systems reuse experience, but stored advice can be flawed or applied in the wrong situation. Team-level success or failure alone cannot reliably show whether a memory needs correction or should not have been used. We propose DiscernMem, a training-free framework that improves both memory quality and memory use. To improve quality, Defect-Aware Memory Refinement (DMR) compares team executions with a single memory and with no memory, diagnoses rule defects, and tests repairs on current and earlier tasks to guard against losing previously useful behavior. To guide appropriate use, Boundary-Learning Meta-Memory (BLM) records each memory's past uses and effects, learning when its owner role should apply or avoid it based on task context and incoming messages. Together, these components help teams correct flawed experience while retaining useful rules that were applied incorrectly. Experiments with Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 on four benchmarks show that DiscernMem achieves the highest average score on AutoGen, CAMEL, and MacNet, exceeding the strongest reported baselines by 0.51-4.32 points. It leads on code generation and symbolic planning across all three systems, including a PDDL score of 37.71 versus 28.48 on CAMEL.

title: Gemini Robotics Embodied Reasoning 2 is now available on Google Cloud
summary:
Earlier this year, we introduced Gemini Robotics 2 — our next-generation intelligence layer enabling robots to think, act, and adapt in the physical world. At the core of this breakthrough is Gemini Robotics Embodied Reasoning 2 (ER 2), a specialized Gemini model that serves as a robot’s high-level brain. Working across any robot embodiment — from stationary arms to full humanoids — Gemini Robotics ER 2 combines advanced spatial and temporal video understanding with long-horizon planning and built-in safety guardrails. This enables robots to converse naturally with humans, orchestrate low-level action models and hardware APIs, execute multi-minute tasks involving hundreds of decisions, and collaborate across multi-robot teams.

Today, we are bringing this same frontier embodied reasoning model to enterprise production environments: Gemini Robotics ER 2 is now available in public preview on the Gemini platform. For the first time, organizations can pair Google DeepMind’s latest embodied reasoning model for robotics with the enterprise-grade security, multi-agent orchestration, and end-to-end lifecycle management of Google Cloud — making it easier to simulate, evaluate, and deploy safe, adaptive physical AI at scale.

Powering physical agents for enterprise robotics

Gemini Robotics ER 2 transforms a robot into a physical agent. The model combines deep spatio-temporal reasoning and long-horizon planning, enabling robots to orchestrate steps to complete a task, self-correct, and generalize to novel situations. To build an agentic setup, developers can declare low-level control interfaces — like Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models or navigation APIs — as tools, and stream multimodal video, audio, or text directly into the model.

Here is what the model delivers for businesses building and operating robotics:

1. Physical task verification, understanding, and self-correction

In physical operations, a robot needs to know whether a step actually succeeded before moving on to the next one. Gemini Robotics ER 2 adapts to new and unfamiliar situations on the fly by reasoning over continuous video feeds. The model:

  • Classifies task progress into binary status, discrete categories, or continuous scores to improve real-time situational awareness and enable real-time adjustment or iteration on failed steps, without restarting an entire workflow.

  • Pinpoints the exact video frame where a critical event occurs (such as when to stop pouring a liquid) with 91.3% accuracy and a 0.96-second mean absolute frame distance, running at 4x the execution speed and a fraction of the compute cost of many larger model categories.

  • It advances our core spatial reasoning capability, including visual question answering and instrument reading. For example, it can read and interpret values across 10+ instrument categories including circular dials, sight glasses, digital displays, linear scales, rulers, and liquid thermometers directly from visual input.

2. One intelligence layer across any embodiments

Gemini Robotics ER 2 orchestrates robots of many shapes and sizes, scaling its intelligence from stationary arms and wheeled rovers to quadrupeds and complex forms. It also unlocks multi-robot collaboration, allowing different types of robots to share a semantic understanding of their workspace, divide labor, and hand off tasks to complete workflows a single machine could not do alone.

3. Agentic tool orchestration and natural language interaction

Gemini Robotics ER 2 thinks about what comes next while simultaneously orchestrating  actions. Developers can declare low-level control interfaces — such as VLA models, navigation APIs, or custom functions — as tools across simulation, real-world robot control, or human tele-operation. Gemini Robotics ER 2 can orchestrate navigation and manipulator movement APIs from natural language commands, allowing the robot to explain its approach while performing an action, and letting operators redirect it without using technical language.

4. Build safe, adaptive physical agents in Google Cloud

Developers and enterprise teams use the Gemini platform to simulate, orchestrate, and manage physical agents, which are then deployed to run directly on physical robots at the edge using Google Cloud's scalable infrastructure:

  • Simulate fast:  Test robot behaviors before touching hardware by running simulations in familiar environments like MuJoCo-Warp and NVIDIA Isaac Sim. Then generate synthetic scenarios with multimodal models and auto-label workcell imagery on the Gemini platform.

  • Train smart: Use Gemini Robotics ER 2's spatial pointing, moment finding, and progress classification to curate and label demonstration videos in Cloud Storage and BigQuery. Then train custom Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models through the Gemini platform, GKE, or Cluster Director.

  • Operate easily: Deploy Gemini Robotics ER 2 workflows on the Gemini platform with enterprise IAM, security controls, and built-in function calling. Offload latency-sensitive local workloads like SLAM and path planning to factory floors with Google Distributed Cloud, and stream fleet telemetry into BigQuery. Explore the full architecture in Google Cloud Physical AI solutions.

How customers are building with Gemini Robotics ER 2 in Gemini platform

“We’ve seen exponential growth in customers using AIVI-Learning every month, and Gemini Robotics ER 2 brings them even more value. Video changes what an inspection can be. Spot isn’t just checking whether something looks right in a moment in time, the ability to apply AI models to video opens a whole new world of possibilities.” 

Marco da Silva, VP and General Manager of Spot at Boston Dynamics

“DeepReach AI is the real-world skills engine for physical AI. Our hardware and AI platform capture how skilled people work all over the world, and turn it into data flywheel for model training. Gemini Robotics ER 2 gives us accurate task understanding of every recording, to help us find data that matters most — faster and at a far greater scale.” 

Chris Liu, Co-founder and CTO at DeepReach

“Advanced reasoning models have the potential to help robots interpret complex environments, plan actions and adapt to changing conditions, opening new possibilities for physical AI. Google’s Gemini Robotics ER 2 model represents an important step in this direction, and we’re excited to be working with Google on exploring how these emerging capabilities can shape the next generation of robotics compute platforms.” 

Barrie Mullins, Senior Director of Arm Total Design for Physical AI, at Arm

“We aim to accelerate materials R&D workflows so our scientists can test more ideas, faster. Most lab automation today relies on rigid scripts for single, isolated tasks. By using Gemini Robotics ER 2, we are giving our robots the visual and physical flexibility to work with our existing infrastructure - whether that’s reading a touchscreen on a legacy microwave reactor that has no API, balancing and loading a centrifuge, or moving samples safely through a busy lab. This is the next level that we aspire to reach. This brings us much closer to self-driving labs that can run full experimental campaigns from synthesis to separation, freeing our researchers to focus on thinking up new ideas for discovering new materials.”

Prof. Loh Xian Jun, Executive Director at ASTAR Institute of Materials Research and Engineering (ASTAR IMRE) and Executive Director of MARVEL-AI”

Get started with Gemini Robotics ER 2 in Gemini platform

Developers and enterprise teams can start building with Gemini Robotics ER 2 today in preview via Model Garden in Gemini platform.

  • Build in Gemini platform: Try in Agent Studio. Visit the Gemini Robotics ER 2 documentation and pricing.

  • Explore the Developer Guides: Check out sample code and bidirectional streaming guides in the Gemini API Robotics documentation.

  • Read the Research: Dive into the benchmarks and safety technical report in the Google DeepMind Gemini Robotics ER 2 announcement.

  • Explore Physical AI on Google Cloud: Visit cloud.google.com/solutions/physical-ai and cloud.google.com/ai to learn how Google Cloud infrastructure supports simulation, training, and deployment.

title: How We Built Our Design Agent
summary: How LangChain built Content Studio, an open-source design agent in Slack that makes on-brand videos, graphics and decks, and the harness that powers it.
story_key: story|title:how we built our design agent
content_excerpt: The promo above was made by Content Studio, our design agent that can create videos, social graphics, recreated UI images, slide decks, and more from just a single prompt in Slack. Every asset the agent produces is written in code. Content Studio was built entirely in-house on Managed Deep Agents . It’s now one of the most widely used GTM agents within our company, but it didn’t start out that way. Early feedback was… not great. We've spent four months teaching Content Studio our taste and design principles, mostly by watching it get things wrong in front of the whole company. This post walks through how our GTM Engineering team worked with our design team to build Content Studio from scratch: what good design means to us, how we taught the agent our taste, and the harness that lets it make anything from a still to a launch film. LangChain moves fast. We have constant product launch campaigns, webinars, blogs and events. Each initiative needs assets, from blog headers and diagrams to decks, videos and ad creatives. Our design team was stretched thin, with repetitive requests crowding out more strategic and innovative work. As a lean startup, we needed a low-friction way for anyone at the company to create high-quality, on-brand work. To address these needs, we built Content Studio, a design agent that lives in Slack. A team member describes what they want and attaches accompanying content or briefs, and the agent returns finished, on-brand files. To build Content Studio, we needed three things: Managed Deep Agents gave us everything we needed to productionize Content Studio inside our company: a managed LangSmith Sandbox , integration with Slack, managed tools, scoped agent memory and scheduling agent runs. This allows a small team to spend its time on the design work, the skills, tools and Slack experience, instead of the plumbing. Before jumping into the build, let’s first address the debate of the century: can AI actually produce good design? The model was already good at execution and could write HTML and CSS, chart specs and animation timelines. However, it didn't have our context, so it reached for familiar patterns, what Anthropic calls “distributional convergence” . The result could look polished and still look like a hundred others, or be beautifully animated and never get its point across. Familiar isn’t always bad, but we wanted our agent to make choices that followed its purpose. Katie Dill , Head of Design at Stripe, makes a helpful comparison

title: claude-code v2.1.312
summary:
What's changed

  • Added oidc.user_id_claim to the Claude apps gateway, to identify people by an id_token claim other than sub, such as Microsoft Entra ID's oid
  • Added click to send: in fullscreen, clicking the "to send now" hint under a queued message sends it right away, as its key does
  • Fixed managed settings and organization policy not being fetched for the rest of the session after signing in from the VS Code extension
  • Fixed Claude overwriting a very large CLAUDE.md, rules file or @-included file in a subdirectory after seeing only its start; Write now asks Claude to read it all or edit in place
  • Fixed per-directory and paths: skills not being found after a Bash cd deeper into a git repository
  • Fixed a rare case where the first reply after resuming a session in the terminal could be missing the next time the session was resumed
  • Fixed a command with an invalid name stopping all commands from loading, which could leave claude -p with no output
  • Fixed the Read tool sometimes failing on PDF pages with "pdftoppm failed: Could not write image" when the clean-up of old session files ran at the same time
  • Fixed the spinner, OpenTelemetry effort values and transcripts naming a newly picked effort level during a task before the model applied it; they now show the level in force
  • Fixed the /model and /effort cache warning saying the re-read waits for your next message; a change made while Claude is working can trigger it sooner
  • Fixed some sessions showing as waiting on you when the last message only mentioned items waiting on you mid-sentence
  • Fixed agent view restoring input text on the next launch after it was cleared with Ctrl+C just before exiting
  • Fixed agent view reopening in shell mode after exiting with Ctrl+D from an empty ! input
  • Fixed vim mode d, c and y with a gj or gk count larger than the lines left deleting or copying text; like Vim, they now only move the cursor
  • Fixed /verify showing a long description meant for Claude in /help and the / command menu instead of a short one
  • Improved the prompt's effort indicator: a change made mid-task now says it may wait for your next message, and the note clears when it no longer applies
  • Improved WebFetch errors in cloud sessions: a host that does not resolve is now explained as possibly outside the allowed network domains, so Claude names the host to allow
  • Changed Bedrock, Vertex, Foundry and Mantle to use the shorter system prompt for model names Claude Code doesn't recognize, such as custom deployment names and inference profile ARNs, even when they front Sonnet or Haiku; set CLAUDE_CODE_SIMPLE_SYSTEM_PROMPT=0 to keep the full prompt
  • Changed automatic model switches after a flagged message to also cover model names Claude Code doesn't recognize, such as custom deployment names; set CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_REFUSAL_FALLBACK=1 to turn them off
  • Changed usage limit messages to call the 5-hour window the "5-hour limit" instead of the "session limit"
  • Changed cloud sessions started from the CLI to get their names and branch names from the server
  • Changed prompt and agent hooks to run at most 24 at a time per session, sub-agents included, plus at most 12 that have waited longer than their event's timeout; a timeout under 1 second now counts as 1 second
  • Changed a subagent's autoCompactWindow to lower the window set by CLAUDE_CODE_AUTO_COMPACT_WINDOW, where it had no effect before; it still never raises that window
  • Changed OpenTelemetry mcp_server.name to report the real name of fixed-URL remote MCP servers declared by plugins from the official Anthropic marketplace, instead of custom
  • Changed Claude Code to stop sending the claude_code.safety_event OpenTelemetry event
  • [VSCode] Fixed sessions ending on a bare exit code when your organization's settings couldn't be loaded or were refused at startup; the tab now says why and offers Retry or Sign in again
  • [VSCode] Changed usage limit resets to show a clock time ("Resets at 3:10 PM") and to say "5-hour limit"
  • [Cloud sessions] Added an effort level to the model picker when you create or edit a routine that runs in the cloud
  • [Cloud sessions] Added a Bash editor with colors, line numbers and a Copy button to the setup script box in cloud environment settings
  • [Cloud sessions] Improved the step shown when Claude adds a repository to a cloud session: opening it now shows a short table of what happened instead of raw JSON
  • [Cloud sessions] Fixed resending an unchanged message after a failed send in a cloud session sometimes running it twice
  • [Cloud sessions] Fixed a failed cloud environment creation showing its error only as a toast outside the open dialog; it now appears inside the dialog
  • [Cloud sessions] Fixed Edit in a routine's menu on the Routines page going to the routine's page without opening its edit dialog
  • [Remote Control] Fixed an unarchived Remote Control session showing as working until a computer reconnected; it now shows as idle
  • [Claude Tag] Improved Claude Tag's retry notice in Slack to name the model in use, or say rate limits were hit, instead of a generic API error
  • [Claude Tag] Fixed a Claude Tag channel's on/off switch and agent settings falling back to workspace defaults when an older private Slack channel goes public and gets a new ID
  • [Claude Tag] Fixed Claude in Slack not replying in channels whose environment has network access set to None
  • [Claude Tag] Fixed Claude in Slack sometimes posting a file in the wrong thread when it was answering in another thread of the same channel
  • [Code Review] Fixed Code Review reviewing an outdated commit, or none at all, when GitHub delivered a push event late; it now reviews the pull request's current commit

title: A Harness Reducing over-Defensive Writing in Agents by Isolating Objections
summary: When expanding a report, writing with agents may introduce a stronger claim than the article makes and then disclaim it. This is called over-defensive writing. We assume that this is because the agent is writing for responding to an adversarial AI reviewer, instead of a human reader. The defensive context may also influnce the consequent when we simply ban defensive writing in the output through prompts. In order to reduce over-defensive writing, we produce a harness that separates the reviewer, filter, and writer. The writer agent receives only the problems choosen by the filter, which is an independent context. We evaluate this harness on 25 business-project drafts expanded into formal reports, the result shows that the defensive propositions decreased from 59 to 2, which is a 96.61\% reduction, no unsupported factual additions were identified while the source-claim retention rises from 80.35% to 93.12%.

title: Evolve on Graph: Self-Evolving Knowledge Graph Reasoning without Question Annotations
summary: Knowledge graphs (KGs) provide reliable external knowledge for multi-hop factual reasoning with large language models (LLMs), yet most KGs in real-world domains such as finance and industry lack question--answer (QA) annotations. Without such annotations, existing methods struggle to improve LLM graph reasoning: training-free agents cannot improve their exploration through interaction; reinforcement learning (RL) agents depend on QA data annotated by humans or synthesized by closed-source models; and training data is typically built offline, so its topology mix is fixed and cannot follow the agent's ability. We propose Evolve on Graph (EoG), a framework that lets an LLM self-evolve its graph reasoning without any QA annotations. Through Graph Self-Play, a single LLM alternates between a Proposer that poses questions and a Solver that answers them. To make questions verifiable, Symbolically Verifiable Topology Synthesis (SVTS) samples reasoning topologies on the KG and executes the corresponding first-order logic queries, yielding topology skeletons with correct and complete answer sets; guided by a skeleton, the Proposer explores the graph to pose a multi-hop question. To let task topologies follow the Solver, a Boundary-Aware Graph Curriculum rewards the Proposer by the Solver's score variance, keeping questions at the Solver's capability boundary so that complex topologies enter training as the Solver improves. On six benchmarks over Freebase, Wikidata, and an industrial KG, EoG consistently outperforms prompting-, retrieval-, and agent-based methods, showing that LLM graph reasoning can improve through self-play without QA annotations. Our code is available at https://github.com/Szy5/EoG

title: Cross-request KV cache exposure in the GLM-5.3 Workers AI model, and our remediation with SGLang
summary: A configuration mismatch in GLM 5.3 on Workers AI triggered an SGLang bug that exposed KV cache pages across requests. Here is how we addressed the issue.
story_key: model:glm|ver:5.3|title:cross request kv cache exposure in the glm 5 3 workers ai model and our remediat
content_excerpt: On September 8, 2026, we were alerted by a security researcher, Gadi Evron from Knostic , to a tenant isolation issue affecting the GLM-5.3 Workers AI model ( @cf/zai-org/glm-5.3 ) starting on August 27, 2026. We have remediated the issue, and we restored the model on September 9. We have confirmed that no other model hosted on Workers AI was affected. Between August 27 and September 9, a small number of customers using the GLM 5.3 Workers AI model received responses that contained data from other customers' requests made to the same model shortly before theirs. In total, 155 responses were affected, all to prompts longer than 681,280 tokens. After excluding our own testing and the researcher's, the requests we identified are consistent in timing and volume with ordinary long-context use, not with someone repeatedly exploiting the bug. We found no evidence of deliberate exploitation. Today we are publishing this report alongside a post from SGLang, the open-source inference engine that we use, as a coordinated disclosure. This post describes the bug that caused this issue, our response timeline, and the subsequent hardening we have conducted on our production SGLang deployments. We also detail our continued efforts with the upstream maintainers of SGLang to address this and similar bugs. GLM is a text generation model from Z.ai that is built for agentic coding workflows; it is one of the many models available through Workers AI. Gadi Evron submitted a report on September 8 through our HackerOne program stating that very long prompts sent to @cf/zai-org/glm-5.3 on Workers AI sometimes returned text that belonged to other users' sessions. Cloudflare reproduced the issue the next morning and took the model offline within 40 minutes of declaring an incident. We then deployed a corrected configuration and a patched inference engine, and restored service the same day. This specific report of cross-request KV cache exposure was the result of two overlapping issues. The first was a misconfiguration of the open-source inference engine, SGLang, used by Cloudflare. We deployed GLM 5.3 with a 1,048,576-token context window, but the KV cache pool on our prefill GPUs only had room for 681,280 tokens. We were aware of this mismatch before launch. We expected the engine to return an error for any prompt it could not process, and our long-context tests returned successful responses, so we did not believe this to be an issue.
